title: Sophie E. Weides
text:
Research
I study how alpine and arctic plants respond to climate change, so which species are moving upslope, which are not, and what happens to plant communities because of these shifts. My PhD at the University of Basel takes a European-scale view of this by combining resurveyed historical vegetation plots all across Europe to which I added with my fieldwork in Norway and Svalbard.
Before Basel I spent five years at the University of Tübingen doing my Bachelor and Master. During my thesis I asked a different kind of question: where, exactly, do grassland plants get their water from? Using stable isotopes, I traced roots to their water sources and found that plants partition the soil more reliably than drought models tend to assume.

title: Outreach
text: Plants are endlessly strange and the public largely doesn’t know it. I try to fix that.

title: Outreach
text:
FameLab Basel 2023

  
  

Three minutes, no slides, one question: where does the water come from? This was my talk at the FameLab Basel 2023 semi-final — a science communication competition where the constraint is the point. Brevity forces you to decide what actually matters.
The talk is about grassland plant roots and stable water isotopes, but really it is about the invisible competition happening just below the surface of any meadow you walk through.

title: Outreach
section: Evening tours at the Botanical Garden of Basel
text:
Evening tours at the Botanical Garden of Basel
Since 2022 I have led public evening tours at the Botanical Garden of the University of Basel — the Feierabendführung series, which runs after work and is open to anyone. No background in botany required.

  Myths, Magic, Medicine — Ethnobotany Through Time
  
    A walk through how humans have used, feared, worshipped, and poisoned each other with plants across millennia. The same species — hemlock, belladonna, St John's wort — has been a cure, a weapon, and a sacrament depending on the century and the culture. The tour is less about memorising Latin names and more about what plants reveal about how people make sense of the world.
  
  
    
      Event page ↗
    
  



  Root Worlds — From Pneumatophores to Walking Trees
  
    Most of what a plant does is invisible. This tour goes underground — into how roots breathe in flooded soils, how certain trees appear to migrate slowly across the landscape, how the belowground competition between neighbours shapes what you see above. It is also, quietly, about what my own research is trying to understand.

title: Outreach
text:
Fieldwork in Svalbard

  
  

A photo diary from fieldwork on the Svalbard archipelago — one of the northernmost places where vascular plants still grow. The trip is part of the data-collection work behind my PhD: resurveying historical vegetation plots to track how alpine plant communities have shifted as the Arctic warms. The Polarsteps log is a way to share the landscape, the logistics, and the plants themselves with anyone curious about what fieldwork in the High Arctic actually looks like.

title: Research
text: I work mostly at large spatial scales — across mountain ranges, elevation gradients, and continents — but fieldwork keeps me honest. The questions I find most interesting tend to be ones where the obvious answer turns out to be wrong.

title: Research
section: PhD: mountain plants in a changing climate
text:
PhD: mountain plants in a changing climate
Europe-wide redistributions of mountain plants during the Anthropocene
University of Basel · 2022 – present
Supervisors: Prof. Sabine Rumpf (Basel) · Prof. John-Arvid Grytnes (Bergen)
Zurich–Basel Plant Science Center
Alpine plants are moving upslope. That much is well established. What is less clear is why some species move and others don’t, whether the whole community shifts together or falls apart, and what actually sets the boundaries of where a plant can live. My thesis tackles these questions from three directions.
What stops alpine plants at their range limits?
Temperature is the usual suspect — but the evidence is patchier than the textbooks suggest. A systematic review I led, published in Ecology and Evolution (2026), synthesised what is actually known about the biotic and abiotic factors that set elevational range limits. The answer is messier and more interesting than “it’s just temperature at the top.”
Do communities homogenise — and does everything happen at once?
When species shift upslope at different rates, the composition of plant communities changes. A chapter currently in preparation for Journal of Vegetation Science asks whether this looks like homogenisation at the landscape scale, and whether dominance shifts happen at the same time as compositional turnover — or whether the two processes decouple.
Svalbard: four decades of change
As a guest PhD student at the University Centre in Svalbard (UNIS) with Prof. Philipp Semenschuk, I resurveyed historical vegetation plots in the Isfjorden area — sites that were first recorded decades ago, in one of the fastest-warming places on Earth. This work was funded by an Arctic Field Grant from the Research Council of Norway (100,000 NOK).

title: Research
section: MSc: where do plants get their water?
text:
MSc: where do plants get their water?
University of Tübingen · 2019–2021
Grassland plants growing side by side do not all drink from the same part of the soil. Using stable water isotope mixing models, I quantified how deep different species reach for water, and whether that changes when the grassland is subjected to experimental drought. The short answer: belowground niche partitioning is more resilient to drought than expected. The work became a first-author paper in Ecology (2024).
A companion study (Kramp et al., Ecology, 2022) showed the other side of the coin — while the partitioning itself holds, individual plant traits do shift: from tolerating drought to avoiding it altogether.

title: Research
text:
BSc: plants under grazing pressure
University of Tübingen · 2016–2019
My BSc thesis looked at how the functional composition of dryland plant communities changes along gradients of grazing intensity. Less a question about individual species, more about what types of plants can persist — and which traits the environment is effectively selecting for.
